title: Magnetism and the motor effect
subtitle: Magnetic fields, electromagnets, the motor effect and Fleming's left-hand rule
lede: Everything in Topic 12, split into two bands. The non-negotiables are poles and the test for a magnet, permanent and induced magnets, field lines, compasses and the Earth, the field around a wire and a solenoid, the motor effect, Fleming's left-hand rule and $F = BIl$. The tricky bits are the chains the marks are on: fields interact → force → accelerates, the magnet test with its expected result, drawing and marking field diagrams, the Earth's field, the left-hand rule on diagrams, $F = BIl$ the hard way, the d.c. motor and the electromagnet investigation. The motor effect (12.10 onwards) is Higher only, badged H; the motor itself (12.14P) is also Physics only, badged P.
howto: Start with the non-negotiables. Do not move on from a section until every practice question is green.
Say every explanation out loud as a chain — current, field around the wire, interacts with the permanent field, resultant force, accelerates, left-hand rule — before you read the one on the page.
Read each explanation, then cover it and say it back. For a definition, the bold words are the ones the mark is for.

Do the practice questions before opening the hint or walkthrough. Calculations in EWAU layout on paper first, then type the answer to check it; write the explanation chains out in full before opening the model answer — the marks are on the links, not the conclusion.
For "explain" and "describe how" questions, write your answer in full sentences, then compare it with the model answer line by line.
Fill in the traffic-light self-check at the end of each section. Anything red or amber is what to revise next.

sections.title: Poles: like repel, unlike attract — and repulsion is the only test

parts.title: The rule and the test
parts.html:
Every magnet has a north-seeking (N) pole and a south-seeking (S) pole; you cannot have one without the other. Like poles repel (N–N, S–S); unlike poles attract (N–S). Magnets also attract magnetic materials — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel — and they attract them whichever pole is nearer, because the magnet induces the opposite pole in the material (N2).

So attraction is not a test: a magnet and a piece of unmagnetised iron attract, and so do two magnets with unlike poles facing. Repulsion is: only two magnets can repel. The June 2025 report (Q7(b)(iv), nails that may or may not be permanently magnetised): one mark for a suitable test, one for a clear statement of the expected result. "Try to pick up a paper clip" scored 1 of 2 — it did not say what the result would mean. The full-mark answer brought one end of a nail up to one end of another, then turned one nail round: if they are not magnets there is attraction in both orientations (or none at all), and never repulsion; if they are magnets, one orientation repels.

parts.title: Is the nail a magnet?
parts.question: A student thinks an iron nail has become a permanent magnet. Describe how she could test this, and state the result she would expect if she is right. (2 marks)
steps: Bring one end of the nail close to one pole of a known magnet (or a compass needle), then reverse the nail and bring the other end to the same pole.
If the nail is a magnet, one end is attracted and the other is repelled. If it is not, both ends are attracted — attraction alone proves nothing, because the magnet would attract any iron.

questions.text: Two bar magnets are placed end to end and they push apart. Which is true?
options: Like poles are facing each other
One of them is not a magnet
questions.explain: Only like poles repel, and only magnets can repel.

questions.text: A steel bar is attracted to the N pole of a magnet. Explain why this does not show that the bar is a magnet. (2)
questions.model:
• A magnet attracts any magnetic material (steel), because it induces the opposite pole in it — so an unmagnetised bar would also be attracted.
  • Only repulsion shows the bar is a magnet, because only two magnets (like poles) can repel.

questions.text: Which observation proves that an object is a permanent magnet?
options: It is attracted to a magnet
It picks up a paper clip
It is repelled by one pole of a magnet
It is heavier than a non-magnet
questions.explain: Repulsion is the only test.

questions.text: Describe a test to show that a bar is not a permanent magnet, and state the expected result. (2)
questions.model:
• Bring each end of the bar in turn to the same pole of a magnet (or a compass needle) — i.e. test both orientations.
  • Expected result if it is not a magnet: attraction in both orientations (no repulsion either way).

questions.text: Which of these is NOT a magnetic material?
questions.explain: Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are magnetic; copper, aluminium and brass are not.

checklist: State that like poles repel and unlike poles attract
Explain why repulsion is the only test for a magnet
Describe a test to show whether an object is a permanent magnet, with the expected result
sections.blurb: Unlike poles attract and like poles repel. A magnet attracts a piece of iron whichever way round it is, so attraction proves nothing — only repulsion shows that an object is itself a magnet.

sections.title: Permanent and induced magnets, and what each is used for
equations: \text{induced: a magnet only while in a field}

parts.title: Permanent versus induced
parts.html:
A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field and keeps it. An induced magnet is a magnetic material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field: the pole nearest the permanent magnet is the opposite pole, so induced magnetism always causes attraction. Take the field away and an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism — that is why it is also called a temporary magnet.

MaterialBehaviourUsed for
Steel (and alloys with cobalt or nickel)hard magnetic material: hard to magnetise, but keeps its magnetismpermanent magnets: compass needles, fridge magnets, the magnets in motors, loudspeakers and generators
Iron (soft iron)soft magnetic material: easy to magnetise, loses its magnetism as soon as the field is removedtemporary magnets: the core of an electromagnet, transformer cores, relays and electric bells — anything that must switch off
Cobalt, nickelmagnetic materials; used mainly in alloys for strong permanent magnetspermanent magnets in headphones, small motors

The exam phrasing: "explain why a steel core would not be suitable for an electromagnet" — because steel keeps its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the electromagnet could not be switched off; iron loses its magnetism, so it can.

parts.title: The 2-mark difference
parts.question: Explain the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet. (2 marks)
steps: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time (it does not need another field to be a magnet).
An induced magnet only becomes a magnet while it is in a magnetic field (of a permanent magnet or an electromagnet), and loses its magnetism when that field is removed.

questions.text: An iron nail is held close to a bar magnet and picks up some paper clips. When the magnet is taken away the clips fall off. Explain these observations. (3)
questions.model:
• In the magnet's field the nail becomes an induced magnet…
  • …so it has poles of its own and attracts the clips (which are themselves induced magnets).
  • Iron is a soft magnetic material, so when the field is removed the nail loses its magnetism and no longer attracts the clips.

questions.text: Why is iron, not steel, used for the core of an electromagnet?
options: Iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the electromagnet can be switched off
questions.explain: Steel would stay magnetised: the electromagnet could not be switched off.

questions.text: Which pole is induced in the end of an iron bar nearest the N pole of a magnet?
questions.explain: The opposite pole is induced, which is why induced magnetism always attracts.

questions.text: Give one use of a permanent magnet and one use of a temporary magnet. (2)
questions.model:
• Permanent: e.g. a compass needle, the magnets in a motor, loudspeaker or generator, a fridge magnet.
  • Temporary: the core of an electromagnet (scrapyard crane, electric bell, relay, circuit breaker), a transformer core.

questions.text: A magnetic material that is easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise is described as…
questions.explain: Soft iron: easy both ways. Steel is 'hard': difficult to magnetise and keeps it.

checklist: Explain the difference between a permanent and an induced magnet
Name the four magnetic materials and say which make permanent and which temporary magnets
Give a use of each kind of material
sections.blurb: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time. An induced (temporary) magnet becomes a magnet only when it is in another magnetic field, and loses most of its magnetism when the field is removed. Steel keeps its magnetism; iron does not.

sections.title: Magnetic field lines: N to S, never crossing, closer means stronger

parts.title: Reading and drawing field lines
parts.html:
A magnetic field is the region around a magnet in which a magnetic material (or another magnet, or a current) experiences a force. The field is drawn as field lines with arrows showing the direction of the force on a N pole placed there: lines leave the N pole, curve round and enter the S pole. The strength of the field is shown by how close the lines are: they are closest at the poles, where the field is strongest, and further apart as you move away.

Between two unlike poles facing each other the lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced from N to S: a uniform field, the same strength and direction everywhere — the field a wire sits in for the motor effect (the motor-effect section, Higher).

The June 2023 report (Q5(a), two magnets): lines drawn overlapping or crossing, or several from the same point on a pole, scored 1 of 2 — "the lines never touch each other and never overlap or cross". Both marks: arrows away from N, lines clean and separate, more of them near the poles.

parts.title: Marking a field diagram
parts.question: A student draws the field around a bar magnet. Her lines leave the N pole, curve round to the S pole, do not cross, and carry arrows — but the arrows point into the N pole. How many of the 2 marks does she get? (2 marks)
steps: Shape: lines from pole to pole, separate, not crossing — the shape mark is earned.
Direction: the arrows must point out of N and into S; hers point the wrong way, so the direction mark is lost. 1 of 2.

questions.text: Field lines around a bar magnet point…
options: from S to N outside the magnet
from N to S outside the magnet
towards the middle of the magnet
questions.explain: Out of N, into S (outside the magnet).

questions.text: State two things the field-line diagram of a magnet tells you, and how. (2)
questions.model:
• The direction of the field: the arrows (the direction a N pole would be pushed, N → S).
  • The strength of the field: how close together the lines are — closer means stronger.

questions.text: Where is the field of a bar magnet strongest?
options: In the middle of the magnet's side
At the poles, where the lines are closest
Between the two poles on the outside
questions.explain: Lines are closest at the poles.

questions.text: Describe the magnetic field between the N pole of one magnet and the S pole of another, placed facing each other a few centimetres apart. (2)
questions.model:
• A uniform field: the lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced…
  • …pointing from the N pole to the S pole; the strength and direction are the same everywhere between them.

questions.text: A student's field diagram has two lines that cross. Why is this wrong?
options: At a crossing point the field would have two directions at once, which is impossible
There should only be one line
Crossing lines mean the magnet is broken
questions.explain: One direction per point: lines never cross or touch.

checklist: Draw the field around a bar magnet with arrows from N to S
Draw the uniform field between two facing unlike poles
Relate the strength of the field to how close the lines are
sections.blurb: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force. Field lines show its direction (the way a free N pole would move: from N to S outside the magnet) and its strength (the closer the lines, the stronger the field). Between two facing unlike poles the field is uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines.

sections.title: Plotting compasses and the Earth's magnetic field

parts.title: The compass and the Earth
parts.html:
Plotting a field: put the magnet on paper, place a plotting compass near one pole and mark a dot at each end of the needle; move the compass so its tail sits on the dot its head made; repeat until you reach the other pole, then join the dots and add an arrow in the direction the N end pointed. Repeat from other starting points for more lines. The compass needle is itself a small magnet, so its N pole points along the field, towards the S pole of the magnet.

The Earth: away from any magnet a compass still points north. A compass only points when there is a magnetic field, so the Earth has a magnetic field; its shape (traced by compasses, with the field running parallel to the ground at the equator and dipping into the ground near the poles) is the shape of a bar magnet's field, so the core of the Earth must be magnetic. Because a compass's N pole is attracted to it, the pole near geographic north is a magnetic S pole. The June 2024 scheme (Q5(a)(ii), 3 marks): "the Earth has a magnetic field"; "the compass needle points in the direction of the field"; "the core is magnetic / as if there were a magnet inside the Earth"; or a point read from the diagram such as "the field goes into the Earth at the north pole".

parts.title: Why a compass points north
parts.question: Explain why a magnetic compass points north, and what this tells us about the Earth. (3 marks)
steps: The compass needle is a small permanent magnet free to turn, so it lines up with any magnetic field it is in, its N pole pointing along the field.
It points north everywhere on Earth, so the Earth has a magnetic field — the Earth's core must be magnetic, acting like a bar magnet inside the Earth.
The needle's N pole is attracted to an unlike pole, so the magnetic pole near geographic north is a magnetic S pole.

questions.text: Describe how to use a plotting compass to show the shape and direction of the field around a bar magnet. (3)
questions.model:
• Place the compass near one pole; mark a dot at each end of the needle.
  • Move the compass so the tail of the needle is on the dot the head made; mark again; repeat to the other pole and join the dots.
  • Add an arrow in the direction the N end pointed; repeat from other starting points to get more lines.

questions.text: The magnetic pole of the Earth near geographic north is…
questions.explain: The compass N pole is attracted to it, and unlike poles attract.

questions.text: A compass needle points north wherever it is taken on the Earth's surface. Explain what this is evidence for. (2)
questions.model:
• A compass only points when it is in a magnetic field, so the Earth has a magnetic field.
  • The field is like a bar magnet's, so the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

questions.text: A plotting compass is placed near the N pole of a bar magnet. Its needle's N end points…
options: away from the magnet's N pole, along the field line
at right angles to the field
questions.explain: Like poles repel: the needle's N end points away from the magnet's N pole, along the field line towards S.

questions.text: At the equator the Earth's field is parallel to the ground; near the poles it dips steeply into the ground. This matches the field of…
options: a bar magnet inside the Earth
questions.explain: The 2024 scheme: 'as if there were a magnet inside the Earth'.

checklist: Describe how to plot a field line with a plotting compass
Explain how a compass shows that the Earth has a magnetic field and that its core must be magnetic
State which magnetic pole is near geographic north, and why a compass points north
sections.blurb: A plotting compass is a small magnet on a pivot: its N pole points along the field at that spot, so moving it step by step traces a field line. Away from any magnet it points north, because the Earth has a magnetic field — evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic, with a magnetic S pole near geographic north.

sections.title: A current makes a magnetic field: the straight wire
equations: \text{stronger: more current, closer to the wire}

parts.title: Showing it, and its shape
parts.html:
Showing that a current has a magnetic effect: pass a straight wire vertically through a horizontal card, place plotting compasses (or sprinkle iron filings) on the card around it, and switch on a large current. The compasses line up in circles round the wire; switch off and they return to pointing north; reverse the current and every compass turns round. The field is a set of concentric circles centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to it.

Direction — the right-hand grip rule: grip the wire with your right hand, thumb along the current (conventional, + to −); your fingers curl the way the field goes. Seen end on, current out of the page (dot) gives an anticlockwise field; current into the page (cross) gives clockwise.

Strength: the field is stronger with a larger current, and weaker further from the wire — the circles are drawn further apart as the distance increases. The June 2025 paper (Q7(c)) gave an unfamiliar equation for B against distance d and expected it to be used like any other; only a few noticed it was an inverse square. You will not be asked to recall any equation for this — just that more current and less distance mean a stronger field.

parts.title: Describing the field
parts.question: A long straight wire carries a current. Describe the magnetic field around it, including how its direction and strength can be changed. (4 marks)
steps: The field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes at right angles to it.
Their direction is given by the right-hand grip rule: thumb along the current, fingers show the field.
Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.
The field is stronger for a larger current and weaker further from the wire (the circles are further apart).

questions.text: Seen end on, a wire carries current into the page (cross). Its magnetic field is…
options: straight lines pointing away from the wire
questions.explain: Right-hand grip: thumb into the page, fingers curl clockwise.

questions.text: Describe how you could show that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field. (3)
questions.model:
• Pass the wire vertically through a card with plotting compasses (or iron filings) on it.
  • With the current on, the compasses line up in circles around the wire; with it off, they point north.
  • Reversing the current reverses the compasses, showing the field direction depends on the current direction.

questions.text: Which change makes the field around a straight wire weaker at a given point?
options: Moving the point closer to the wire
Moving the point further from the wire
questions.explain: Strength falls with distance; reversing only changes direction.

questions.text: State two factors that affect the strength of the magnetic field around a long straight wire. (2)
questions.model:
• The size of the current (larger current, stronger field).
  • The distance from the wire (further away, weaker field).

questions.text: A plotting compass next to a wire turns round when the current is reversed. This shows that…
options: the direction of the field depends on the direction of the current
the wire has become a permanent magnet
questions.explain: Field direction follows the current direction.

checklist: Describe how to show that a current produces a magnetic field
Draw the field around a straight wire and give its direction from the current direction
State the two things the strength of the field depends on
sections.blurb: A wire carrying a current has a magnetic field around it: concentric circles centred on the wire. The direction comes from the right-hand grip rule (thumb along the current, fingers curl with the field) and reverses when the current reverses. The field is stronger with a larger current and closer to the wire.

sections.title: The solenoid: fields add inside, cancel outside

parts.title: Why a coil beats a wire
parts.html:
A solenoid is a wire wound into a long coil. Each turn has the circular field of N5. Inside the coil the fields of all the turns point the same way along the axis, so they add together to give a very strong, almost uniform field (straight, parallel, equally spaced lines along the centre). Outside the coil the fields of neighbouring turns point in opposite directions and largely cancel, so the field there is weaker; what is left has the same shape as a bar magnet's field, with a N pole at one end and a S pole at the other. The spec's own words (12.9): the fields from individual coils "add together to form a very strong almost uniform field along the centre" and "cancel to give a weaker field outside".

An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core, which becomes an induced magnet and makes the field far stronger — and switches off with the current (N2). Stronger electromagnet: more current, more turns (per unit length), an iron core. Reverse the current and the poles swap.

parts.title: The 3-mark explanation
parts.question: Explain why the magnetic field inside a solenoid is much stronger than the field around a single straight wire carrying the same current. (3 marks)
steps: Each turn of the solenoid produces its own magnetic field (circles around the wire).
Inside the coil the fields of all the turns point the same way, so they add together…
…giving a strong, almost uniform field along the centre — many turns' worth of field in the same place.

questions.text: The field outside a solenoid is weak because…
options: the fields of neighbouring turns point in opposite directions there and cancel
field lines cannot leave a coil
questions.explain: Cancel outside, add inside.

questions.text: Describe the magnetic field inside and outside a solenoid. (3)
questions.model:
• Inside: strong and almost uniform — straight, parallel, equally spaced lines along the axis.
  • Outside: weaker…
  • …with the shape of a bar magnet's field: a N pole at one end, a S pole at the other.

questions.text: Which does NOT increase the strength of an electromagnet?
options: Using thinner card for the coil to sit on
questions.explain: Turns, current and core are the three.

questions.text: An electromagnet is used in a scrapyard crane to lift and drop cars. Explain why it has a soft iron core and not a steel one. (2)
questions.model:
• Soft iron becomes an induced magnet in the coil's field, making the electromagnet much stronger, and loses its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off — so the car can be dropped.
  • Steel would keep its magnetism when the current is off, so the car could not be released.

questions.text: Reversing the current in a solenoid…
options: swaps its N and S poles
has no effect on the field
questions.explain: Field direction follows current direction, so the poles swap.

checklist: Explain why the field inside a solenoid is strong and almost uniform
Explain why the field outside is weaker, and describe its shape
State three ways to make an electromagnet stronger
sections.blurb: A solenoid is a long coil of wire. Inside it, the fields of all the turns point the same way and add up to a strong, almost uniform field along the axis; outside, they largely cancel, leaving a weaker field with the shape of a bar magnet's. An iron core makes it an electromagnet.

sections.title: The motor effect: two fields interact, so there is a force on the wire

parts.title: The chain to write every time
parts.html:
A current-carrying wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force — the motor effect. Why: the current creates a magnetic field around the wire; this interacts with the permanent magnet's field; where the two point the same way the field is stronger, where they oppose it is weaker, and the result is a resultant force on the wire from the strong side towards the weak side. By Newton's third law an equal and opposite force acts on the magnet. The standard explanation, in the steps the marks are on:

  1. There is a current in the wire.
  2. This creates a magnetic field around the wire.
  3. This interacts with the permanent magnetic field.
  4. This causes a resultant force on the wire, so the wire accelerates.
  5. You can find the direction of the force using Fleming's left-hand rule.

Two things the examiners want and students leave out: the force is due to the interaction between the two magnetic fields (12.11) — not "the magnet pushes the wire"; and the chain ends with what happens: a resultant force, so the wire accelerates (or, if it is held, is pushed against what holds it). The June 2023 report (Q5(b), one magnet floating above another): "repulsion" alone scored one mark; the second mark needed "the interaction between the two magnetic fields" — the same idea.

The force is at right angles to both the current and the field (direction from Fleming's left-hand rule, N8). It is largest when the wire is at right angles to the field and zero when the wire is parallel to it. It reverses if either the current or the field is reversed, and grows with more current, a stronger field or more wire in the field (N9).

parts.title: Why the wire jumps
parts.question: A straight wire is placed between the poles of a horseshoe magnet. When the current is switched on the wire jumps out of the magnet. Explain why. (4 marks)
steps: There is a current in the wire. This creates a magnetic field around the wire.
This interacts with the permanent magnetic field.
This causes a resultant force on the wire, so the wire accelerates — out of the magnet.
You can find the direction of the force using Fleming's left-hand rule (it is at right angles to both the current and the field).

questions.text: A wire carrying a current is placed at right angles to the field between two magnets. Explain why there is a force on the wire. (3)
questions.model:
• The current in the wire creates a magnetic field around the wire.
  • This field interacts with the permanent magnetic field of the magnets.
  • The interaction causes a resultant force on the wire, so the wire accelerates.

questions.text: A wire carrying a current experiences a force from a magnet. What force acts on the magnet?
options: None — magnets do not feel forces
A force in the same direction as the force on the wire
questions.explain: Newton's third law: the magnet feels an equal and opposite force.

questions.text: When is the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field zero?
options: When the wire is at right angles to the field
When the wire is parallel to the field
questions.explain: Parallel: no force. At right angles: maximum.

questions.text: A student writes: "The magnet pushes the wire." Rewrite the explanation so that it earns the 'interaction' mark. (2)
questions.model:
• The current in the wire produces its own magnetic field…
  • …which interacts with the magnet's field; the force on the wire is due to this interaction between the two magnetic fields.

questions.text: Which change makes the force on the wire larger without changing its direction?
options: Reversing the magnetic field (turning the magnet round)
Turning the wire so it lies along the field
questions.explain: Doubling the current doubles the force and keeps its direction. Reversing either reverses it; a wire along the field feels no force at all.

checklist: Write the five-step chain for the motor effect on a wire
State that an equal and opposite force acts on the magnet
Explain that the force is due to the interaction between two magnetic fields
sections.blurb: A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a force, and an equal and opposite force acts on the magnet. The force is the interaction between the wire's own magnetic field and the magnet's field. The standard five-step chain below is the one to write every time.

sections.title: Fleming's left-hand rule: thumb force, first finger field, second finger current

parts.title: The rule
parts.html:
Use the left hand. Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger so that each is at right angles to the other two. Then: First finger = Field, pointing the way the field lines go (N to S); seCond finger = Current, pointing the way the conventional current goes (+ to −, not the electron flow); thuMb = Motion, the direction of the force on the wire (and so the way it moves). The three are mutually perpendicular: the rule represents "the relative directions of the force, the current and the magnetic field for cases where they are mutually perpendicular" (12.12). If the current is parallel to the field there is no force and the rule does not apply.

In the exam the picture is usually end on: a dot is current out of the page, a cross is current into the page. Point the second finger at yourself for a dot, away for a cross, line the first finger up with the field arrows, and read the thumb. Reversing the current or the field reverses the force; reversing both leaves it unchanged. The June 2024 scheme (Q5(b)(ii)): to reverse the force on a coil, "any clear action that will reverse the current" (swap the battery connections) or "any clear action that will reverse the poles" (turn the magnet round).

parts.title: Reading a diagram
parts.question: A wire between the poles of a magnet carries a current out of the page. The magnetic field points from left to right. Find the direction of the force on the wire. (2 marks)
steps: First finger along the field: pointing to the right. Second finger along the current: pointing out of the page, towards you.
With both in place the thumb points upwards — the force on the wire is up the page.

questions.text: In Fleming's left-hand rule the first finger represents…
questions.explain: First finger: Field. Second: Current. Thumb: Motion (force).

questions.text: A wire carries current into the page; the field points from left to right. The force on the wire is…
questions.explain: Second finger away from you, first finger right: thumb points down.

questions.text: State two ways of reversing the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. (2)
questions.model:
• Reverse the current (e.g. swap the connections to the battery).
  • Reverse the magnetic field (e.g. turn the magnet round so the poles swap).

questions.text: A wire lies parallel to the field lines between two magnets and carries a current. The force on it is…
questions.explain: The rule needs the current and field at right angles; parallel means no force.

questions.text: The second finger must point in the direction of…
questions.explain: Conventional current. Using electron flow gives the opposite answer.

questions.text: The field points up the page and the force on a wire is out of the page (towards you). The current in the wire is…
questions.explain: Set first finger up, thumb towards you: the second finger points right. (Check: field up, current right, force out of the page.)

checklist: State what each of the three digits represents
Use the rule to find the missing one of force, field and current on a diagram
State that the rule applies when the three directions are mutually perpendicular
sections.blurb: Hold the left hand with thumb, first finger and second finger at right angles to each other. First finger along the field (N to S), second finger along the conventional current (+ to −), and the thumb gives the direction of the force (the motion). It only applies when the current and field are at right angles.

sections.title: The size of the force: F = B I l

parts.title: The equation and its units
parts.html:
For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field: force (N) = magnetic flux density (T) × current (A) × length (m), $F = B I l$. Magnetic flux density $B$ is the strength of the field, in tesla (T); 1 T = 1 N/A m, i.e. the field in which 1 m of wire carrying 1 A feels 1 N — a large unit, so exam fields are usually tenths of a tesla or millitesla. $l$ is the length of wire in the field, in metres. The equation is on the equation list, so the marks are for choosing it, converting cm to m and mA to A, substituting and rearranging. The June 2023 report (Q5(c)(ii)): almost every candidate selected and used it correctly; the June 2024 scheme (Q5(b)(iii)) gave one mark for "rearrangement and substitution" and one for the evaluation, 0.58 T, with full marks for a correct answer without working.

Three traps: leaving the length in centimetres (force 100 times too big); using the whole length of a wire when only part of it is in the field; and forgetting the force is zero for a wire parallel to the field, whatever $B$, $I$ and $l$ are.

parts.title: Finding B
parts.question: A wire of length 5.0 cm carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a magnetic field. The force on it is 0.030 N. Calculate the magnetic flux density. (3 marks)
steps: Rearrange $F = B I l$: $B = F \div (I \times l) = 0.030 \div (2.5 \times 0.050)$.

questions.text: A wire 0.20 m long carries 4.0 A at right angles to a field of flux density 0.15 T. Calculate the force on it.
questions.hint: $F = B \times I \times l$ — all three already in base units.

questions.text: A 12 cm length of wire carries a current of 0.50 A across a field of 0.80 T. Calculate the force.
The force on a 0.40 m wire in a field of 0.25 T is 0.30 N. Calculate the current.
A wire carries 1.5 A. A 25 cm length of it lies in a field of 0.040 T at right angles. Calculate the force in millinewtons.
Which is a correct unit for magnetic flux density?
questions.explain: 1 T = 1 N/A m, from B = F ÷ (I l).

checklist: Use $F = BIl$ for a wire at right angles to the field
Give the unit of magnetic flux density and convert cm and mA before substituting
Rearrange for B, I or l
sections.blurb: For a wire at right angles to the field, the force is magnetic flux density × current × length of wire in the field: $F = BIl$, with $B$ in tesla; the equation is on the list, so the skill is choosing it, converting cm to m, and rearranging for B, I or l.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this
Magnetic materialA material that is attracted by a magnet and can be magnetised: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel."metal" — copper and aluminium are not magnetic
Permanent magnetA magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time (steel, or alloys of cobalt and nickel)."a strong magnet"
Induced (temporary) magnetA magnetic material that becomes a magnet only while it is in a magnetic field, and loses its magnetism when the field is removed (soft iron)."a weak magnet"
Magnetic fieldThe region around a magnet (or a current) in which a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force."the magnetism"
Field lineA line showing the direction of the field (the direction of the force on a N pole: N to S); closer lines mean a stronger field; lines never cross."the path of the magnet"
Uniform fieldA field with the same strength and direction everywhere: parallel, equally spaced lines (between unlike poles; inside a solenoid)."a straight field"
SolenoidA long coil of wire; with a current it has a field like a bar magnet's, strong and uniform inside."an electromagnet" (only with a core)
ElectromagnetA solenoid with a soft iron core: a magnet that can be switched on and off with the current."a magnet with wire"
Right-hand grip ruleGrip the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current: the fingers curl the way the field goes.mixing it up with the left-hand rule
Motor effectA current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, due to the interaction between the two magnetic fields."a motor spins"
Fleming's left-hand ruleFirst finger Field (N → S), second finger Current (+ → −), thumb Motion (force), all at right angles.right hand; electron flow
Magnetic flux density, BThe strength of a magnetic field: the force per unit current per unit length on a wire at right angles to it; unit tesla, T (= N/A m)."the amount of magnetism"
Split-ring commutatorThe two half-rings on a d.c. motor's axle that reverse the current in the coil every half turn, so the coil keeps turning the same way."the thing that connects the wires"

questions.text: State what is meant by a magnetic field. (1)
questions.model: • The region around a magnet (or current) in which a magnetic material (or another magnet) experiences a force.

questions.text: State what is meant by an induced magnet. (1)
questions.model: • A magnetic material that becomes a magnet only while it is in a magnetic field (and loses its magnetism when the field is removed).

questions.text: Which is the best definition of a permanent magnet?
options: A magnet that is very strong
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time
questions.explain: Its own field, always.

questions.text: State what is meant by a uniform magnetic field, and where one is found. (2)
questions.model:
• A field with the same strength and direction at every point (parallel, equally spaced lines).
  • Between two unlike poles facing each other, or inside a solenoid.

questions.text: State what is meant by the motor effect. (1)
questions.model: • A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (due to the interaction of the two fields).

questions.text: Magnetic flux density is measured in…
questions.explain: Tesla, T (= N/A m).

checklist: Define magnetic material, permanent and induced magnet
Define magnetic field, field line, uniform field, solenoid and electromagnet
Define the motor effect, magnetic flux density and the commutator
sections.blurb: One-mark definitions in the form of words the mark schemes credit. The bold words are the ones the marks are attached to. The last four terms (motor effect onwards) are Higher only, and the commutator is Physics only as well.

sections.title: Explaining why magnets move: fields interact → force on X → X accelerates
equations: \text{fields interact} \rightarrow \text{force on X} \rightarrow \text{X accelerates (or is held)}

parts.title: The chain, and where the marks are
parts.html:
SituationChain (each link a mark)
Magnet X placed near magnet Y, like poles facing, X free to movethe magnetic field of X interacts with the field of Y → like poles repel, so there is a force on X directed away from Y → the force is unbalanced, so X accelerates away from Y
Unlike poles facingfields interact → unlike poles attract, so a force on X towards Y → X accelerates towards Y
A magnet floating above another (like poles facing) — June 2023 Q5(b)the fields interact → like poles repel, so there is an upward (repulsive) force on the upper magnet → this force is equal to its weight (the downward force of gravity), so the forces are balanced and the magnet stays still (equilibrium)
A piece of iron near a magnetthe magnet's field induces the opposite pole in the near end of the iron → unlike poles attract, so a force on the iron towards the magnet → the iron accelerates towards the magnet (so iron is always attracted, never repelled)

The June 2023 report on the floating magnet: answers that mentioned fields only to say "repulsion" "can score one mark for repulsion but not another mark for the interaction between fields". Full marks: the interaction of the two magnetic fields, an upward repulsive force, and that it balances gravity. One answer with interaction and repulsion but no gravity and no equilibrium lost marks. The link between the force and what happens — accelerates, or balanced so it stays — is the same link the examiners look for with charges (Topic 11 T1) and with forces generally (Topic 2).

parts.title: The floating magnet
parts.question: Two ring magnets are threaded on a wooden rod with like poles facing. The upper magnet floats above the lower one. Explain why it floats. (3 marks)
steps: The magnetic field of the upper magnet interacts with the magnetic field of the lower magnet.
Like poles are facing, so they repel: there is an upward force on the upper magnet.
This upward force is equal to the weight of the upper magnet, so the forces on it are balanced and it stays still.

questions.text: A bar magnet is placed on a smooth table with its N pole facing the N pole of a fixed magnet. It moves away. Explain why. (2)
questions.model:
• Like poles repel, so there is a force on the free magnet directed away from the fixed one.
  • The force is unbalanced, so the magnet accelerates away. (Higher: add that the force arises because the two magnets' fields interact.)

questions.text: A student explains the floating magnet by writing "like poles repel so it floats". State two things the answer is missing. (2)
questions.model:
• That the force comes from the interaction between the two magnetic fields.
  • That the upward repulsive force balances the weight (gravity) of the upper magnet, so it is in equilibrium.

questions.text: A magnet X is released near a fixed magnet Y with unlike poles facing. Which is the best description of what happens?
options: There is a force on X towards Y, so X accelerates towards Y
X moves at a steady speed towards Y
questions.explain: Force on X, towards Y, so X accelerates — name the object, the direction and the acceleration.

questions.text: An unmagnetised iron nail is placed near a magnet and moves towards it. Explain why the nail is attracted whichever pole of the magnet faces it. (3)
questions.model:
• The magnet's field induces magnetism in the nail, with the opposite pole at the end nearest the magnet.
  • Unlike poles attract, so there is a force on the nail towards the magnet…
  • …so the nail accelerates towards the magnet. Either pole of the magnet induces the opposite pole, so it is attraction every time.

questions.text: Why does a floating magnet stay at a fixed height rather than keep rising?
options: The upward magnetic force equals its weight, so the resultant force is zero
questions.explain: Balanced forces: it stays at the height where repulsion equals weight.

checklist: Write the chain for a magnet moving away from (or towards) another
Write the chain for a magnet held still: the magnetic force balances the weight
Say which object the force acts on, and which way
sections.blurb: "Explain why the magnet moves away" is not answered by "like poles repel". The marks are on the chain: the two magnetic fields interact (the Higher-only link, 12.11), so there is a force on the magnet (say which one, and which way), so it accelerates — or, if it floats or is held, the force balances another force. Same shape as the Topic 11 chain for charges.

sections.title: Is it a magnet? Designing the test and stating the result

parts.title: The three possibilities
parts.html:
ObjectBring one pole of a known magnet to each end in turnWhy
Permanent magnetone end is attracted, the other is repelledit has its own poles; like poles repel
Magnetic material (unmagnetised iron, steel)attracted at both ends, never repelledthe known magnet induces the opposite pole whichever end is nearer
Non-magnetic material (copper, plastic)no force either wayit cannot be magnetised

So the test is: approach both ends with the same pole of a known magnet (or a compass needle — its N end is a known pole), and look for repulsion. The June 2025 report (Q7(b)(iv)): "one mark for a suitable test and one for a clear statement of the expected result"; "trying to pick up a paper clip … earned 1 of 2, since it did not show what the result would mean" — an induced magnet also picks up paper clips while the field is there. The full-mark answer reversed one nail and looked for no repulsion in either orientation (any force was attraction both ways, or there was none). Why a paper-clip test fails for a nail that has just been in a field: it may be a weak induced magnet for a while; only repulsion is proof of a permanent magnet.

parts.title: Nails after the electromagnet
parts.question: Nails were picked up by an electromagnet. A student claims the nails have become permanent magnets. Describe a test to check this and state the result expected if she is wrong. (2 marks)
steps: Hold one nail by its middle and bring one end of a second nail (or one pole of a known magnet) to each end of it in turn, i.e. test both orientations.
If the nails are not permanent magnets there is no repulsion in either orientation (any attraction is the same at both ends, or there is none); a permanent magnet would be repelled at one end.

questions.text: A bar is attracted to both poles of a magnet. It is…
questions.explain: Attraction at both ends, no repulsion: magnetic material, not a magnet.

questions.text: Explain why a bar that picks up a paper clip is not necessarily a permanent magnet. (2)
questions.model:
• The bar might be an induced (temporary) magnet — a magnetic material still in, or just out of, a magnetic field.
  • Only repulsion by a known magnet proves it is a permanent magnet, because only two magnets can repel.

questions.text: Describe how a compass could be used to find out whether a steel rod is a permanent magnet. State the expected results. (3)
questions.model:
• Bring the N end of the compass needle to one end of the rod, then to the other end.
  • If the rod is a permanent magnet the needle's N end is attracted to one end and repelled by the other.
  • If it is not, the needle's N end is attracted to both ends (induced magnetism) — no repulsion.

questions.text: A student's answer to 'test whether the nail is a magnet' is: "Hold it near some iron filings and see if they stick." What is wrong?
options: Filings would also stick to an induced magnet, so sticking does not show it is permanent — and no expected result is stated
questions.explain: Test needs repulsion, and the expected result must be stated.

questions.text: Two bars look identical. One is a magnet, one is unmagnetised iron. Bringing the END of bar A to the MIDDLE of bar B gives strong attraction; bringing the end of B to the middle of A gives almost none. Which is the magnet?
questions.explain: A magnet's poles are at its ends, and its middle is weak: A's end attracts B's middle strongly, so A is the magnet (B's end at A's weak middle does little).

checklist: Design a test that distinguishes a magnet from a magnetic material
State the expected result for each possibility
Explain why picking up a paper clip is not enough
sections.blurb: Three kinds of object look the same: a permanent magnet, an unmagnetised magnetic material, and a non-magnetic material. One compass or one known magnet tells them apart — if you test both ends and say what each result means. The 2025 examiners gave one mark for the test and one for the expected result.

sections.title: Drawing and marking field diagrams

parts.title: The five patterns and the marking
parts.html:
FieldShapeDirectionSee
Bar magnetloops from one pole round to the other; straight line out of each end; closest at the polesout of N, into SN3
N facing Snearly straight, parallel lines across the gap (uniform between the poles), curving outward at the edgesN → S across the gapN3
N facing N (or S facing S)lines curve away from each other; a neutral point midway where the field is zero (no lines)out of both N poles—
Straight wireconcentric circles centred on the wire, further apart with distanceright-hand grip ruleN5
Solenoidstraight, parallel, equally spaced inside; bar-magnet loops outsidethrough the inside and out of the N endN6

Marking (June 2023 Q5(a) and the general schemes): the shape mark needs lines that do not cross, touch or overlap, that start and end on poles (or form closed circles round a wire), and that are closer near the poles; several lines from the same point on a pole lost it. The direction mark needs arrows on the lines, out of N and into S — at least one arrow on each line, all consistent. No arrows at all: no direction mark. Arrows the wrong way: no direction mark, even with a perfect shape. Field lines inside the magnet are not needed at GCSE and are ignored if drawn.

parts.title: Two N poles
parts.question: Two bar magnets are placed in a line with their N poles 3 cm apart. Draw the magnetic field between them, and describe it. (3 marks)
steps: Lines leave each N pole and curve away from the other magnet — none joins the two N poles, because like poles repel.
Midway between the poles there is a neutral point where the two fields cancel: the field is zero there, so no line passes through it.
Arrows out of both N poles (and, if the S poles are shown, round to them). Description: the field is weak between the poles and zero at the neutral point; the lines are furthest apart there.

questions.text: A diagram of the field around a bar magnet has no arrows on any line. The shape is perfect. Marks out of 2?
questions.explain: No arrows, no direction mark.

questions.text: Describe the magnetic field pattern between the S pole of one magnet and the S pole of another placed facing it. (2)
questions.model:
• The lines curve away from each other: they enter each S pole from the sides and do not run straight across the gap.
  • There is a neutral point midway between the poles where the field is zero.

questions.text: Which is NOT a reason for losing the shape mark on a bar-magnet field diagram?
options: Lines are closer together near the poles
Several lines leave the same point on the pole
questions.explain: Closer near the poles is correct — it shows the stronger field.

questions.text: A student draws the field around a straight wire as straight lines pointing away from the wire. Explain what is wrong and what she should draw. (2)
questions.model:
• The field of a straight wire is circles centred on the wire, not radial lines — the radial pattern is an electric field (Topic 11).
  • Draw concentric circles, further apart with distance, with arrows given by the right-hand grip rule (clockwise for current into the page).

questions.text: Inside a solenoid the field lines should be drawn…
questions.explain: Uniform inside: straight, parallel, equally spaced.

checklist: Draw the five standard field patterns
Mark a field diagram: say what scores and what loses the mark
Describe the field between two like poles
sections.blurb: A field-diagram question is usually two marks: one for the shape, one for the direction. The shapes to know are the bar magnet, two magnets facing (N–S and N–N), the straight wire, and the solenoid. What loses the mark: lines that cross or touch, no arrows, arrows into N, lines that stop in mid-air.

sections.title: The Earth as a magnet: reading the field and the evidence
equations: \text{compass points north} \Rightarrow \text{Earth has a field} \Rightarrow \text{core is magnetic}

parts.title: Reading the Earth's field
parts.html:
Treat the Earth as a bar magnet with its S pole near geographic north and its N pole near geographic south (N4 figure). Then at any point: lines come out of the Earth near geographic south, run parallel to the surface, pointing north, at the equator, and go into the Earth near geographic north. A compass at any point lines up with the field there: on the surface its N end points north; a compass free to tilt dips downwards in the northern hemisphere.

The June 2024 scheme (Q5(a)): at the point on the surface near the equator the arrow pointed up the page (along the surface towards north); at the other marked point the arrow pointed the other way, down the page — read each one from the loop it lies on: outside the Earth the lines run from the magnetic N pole (geographic south) round to the magnetic S pole (geographic north), and inside the Earth they run back the other way. Judged by eye, within 10°. For the evidence (3 marks, any three): the Earth has a magnetic field; a compass needle points along the field; the field goes into the Earth at the north pole / comes out at the south; it runs parallel to the surface at the equator; the core is magnetic — "as if there were a magnet inside the Earth".

The naming twist: the end of a compass needle that points north is its north-seeking pole, a magnetic N pole. It is attracted north, and unlike poles attract, so the thing attracting it — the Earth's pole near geographic north — is a magnetic S pole. Students lose this mark by writing "the Earth's north pole is a north pole".

parts.title: The 3-mark evidence
parts.question: Explain how the behaviour of a magnetic compass provides evidence that the core of the Earth is magnetic. (3 marks)
steps: A compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with a magnetic field; it points north everywhere, so the Earth has a magnetic field.
The shape of that field — parallel to the ground at the equator, dipping into the ground near the poles — is the shape of a bar magnet's field.
So the field must come from inside the Earth: the core must be magnetic, as if there were a bar magnet in it.

questions.text: At a point just above the equator, the Earth's magnetic field points…
options: parallel to the surface, towards geographic north
parallel to the surface, towards geographic south
questions.explain: Along the surface, from the magnetic N pole (south) to the magnetic S pole (north).

questions.text: Explain why the magnetic pole of the Earth near the geographic north pole is a magnetic south pole. (2)
questions.model:
• The N (north-seeking) pole of a compass needle points towards geographic north — it is attracted there.
  • Unlike poles attract, so the pole it is attracted to must be a magnetic S pole.

questions.text: Near the geographic north pole, the Earth's field lines…
questions.explain: Into the magnetic S pole, which is near geographic north.

questions.text: Give three pieces of evidence, from the behaviour of compasses, that the Earth has a magnetic field like that of a bar magnet. (3)
questions.model:
• A compass points north everywhere (it only points when in a field).
  • The field is parallel to the surface at the equator and dips into the ground near the poles (goes in at one pole, out at the other).
  • The naming: a compass's N end is attracted towards geographic north, consistent with a magnetic S pole there — the pattern of a bar magnet inside the Earth.

questions.text: Why is a compass used in navigation?
options: Its needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, so it always shows the direction of north
questions.explain: Lines up with the Earth's field: a fixed reference direction.

checklist: Give the field direction at points around the Earth from the bar-magnet picture
List the evidence that the Earth has a magnetic field and a magnetic core
Explain why the pole near geographic north is a magnetic S pole
sections.blurb: The 2024 paper drew the Earth with its field and asked for the field direction at marked points, then for the evidence that the Earth has a magnetic field. The direction at any point follows the bar-magnet picture: out of the magnetic N pole (near geographic south), round, into the magnetic S pole (near geographic north); parallel to the surface at the equator.

sections.title: Using Fleming's left-hand rule on diagrams: dots, crosses and the missing direction

parts.title: The three cases
parts.html:
Method: (1) check the current and field are at right angles — if the wire runs along the field, the answer is no force and you stop; (2) point the first finger along the field, N to S; (3) point the second finger along the current — towards you for a dot, away from you for a cross; (4) the thumb gives the force. To find the current instead, set the first finger (field) and thumb (force) and read the second finger. To find the field, set thumb and second finger and read the first.

Reversing: reversing the current reverses the force; reversing the field reverses the force; reversing both leaves it as it was. The June 2024 scheme (Q5(b)(ii)): "swap the battery connections around" or "turn the magnet around". A common slip is to use the right hand (which gives the opposite answer) or to point the second finger along the electron flow — the rule uses conventional current, + to −.

parts.title: Finding the current
parts.question: A wire between the poles of a magnet experiences a force up the page. The field points from right to left. Find the direction of the current. (2 marks)
steps: First finger along the field: pointing left. Thumb along the force: pointing up.

The second finger then points into the page, away from you — the current is into the page (a cross). Check against the reference case: field right with current out gives force up; reversing the field alone would give force down, so to keep the force up the current must be reversed too — into the page.

questions.text: Field from left to right; current out of the page (dot). Force on the wire?
questions.explain: First finger right, second finger towards you, thumb up.

questions.text: Field from left to right; current into the page (cross). Force?
questions.explain: Reversing the current reverses the force: down.

questions.text: Field from right to left; current into the page (cross). Force?
questions.explain: Reversing both the field and the current (compared with q1) leaves the force as it was: up.

questions.text: Field down the page; force on the wire to the right. The current is…
questions.explain: First finger down, thumb right: the second finger points towards you — out of the page. (Check: field down, current out, force right.)

questions.text: Field from left to right; the wire runs from left to right too, carrying a current. Force?
questions.explain: Current parallel to the field: no force.

questions.text: A wire between two magnets is pushed upwards when the current is switched on. State and explain two separate changes that would each make it move downwards instead. (4)
questions.model:
• Reverse the current (swap the connections to the supply)…
  • …because the force reverses when the current reverses (the second finger reverses, so the thumb reverses).
  • Reverse the field (turn the magnet round / swap the poles)…
  • …because the force reverses when the field reverses (the first finger reverses, so the thumb reverses). Doing both would leave it moving up.

checklist: Find the force direction from a dot-or-cross diagram
Find the current direction given the field and the force
Recognise the no-force case and the two ways of reversing the force
sections.blurb: The exam gives two of the three directions and asks for the third, usually with the wire end on. The method is the same every time: set the first finger along the field, the second along the current, read the thumb; and check first that the current and field are at right angles.

sections.title: F = BIl the hard way: rearranging, the length in the field, and unfamiliar equations

parts.title: Where the extra marks hide
parts.html:
TwistWhat to do
Length given in cm, current in mA, force in mNconvert to m, A and N before substituting; write the conversion as a line of working
A long wire, only part of it between the poles$l$ is the length inside the field — usually the width of the magnet or the pole pieces, not the whole wire
A coil of N turns with one side in the fieldthe force on that side is $N$ times the force on one wire: $F = B I l N$ — the question will say so, or ask for the force on one wire
Current not given, but pd and resistance arefind $I = V / R$ first (Topic 10), then $F = B I l$
An unfamiliar equation is givenJune 2025 Q7(c): an equation linking $B$ and distance $d$ — substitute and rearrange exactly as you would for $F = B I l$; finding the constant and stopping scored 1 of 3
Wire parallel to the field$F = 0$ — the equation only applies at right angles

The June 2024 scheme (Q5(b)(iii), 2 marks): "rearrangement and substitution" (1), "evaluation" (1) — 0.58 T, or anything rounding to 0.6 T; full marks for the correct answer alone. Show the rearranged equation with numbers in it: that line is a mark on its own if the arithmetic goes wrong.

parts.title: The 2024-style flux density
parts.question: A wire carries a current of 1.2 A. A 5.0 cm length of it lies at right angles to a magnetic field, and the force on the wire is 0.035 N. Calculate the magnetic flux density. (2 marks)
steps: Convert: $l = 5.0$ cm $= 0.050$ m. Rearrange and substitute: $B = F \div (I l) = 0.035 \div (1.2 \times 0.050)$.
$B = 0.035 \div 0.060 = 0.58$ T (anything rounding to 0.6 T).

questions.text: A wire 60 cm long is held across a magnet whose poles are 4.0 cm wide. The current is 3.0 A and the flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
questions.hint: Only the length between the poles is in the field.
walkthrough: $l = 4.0$ cm $= 0.040$ m — the length in the field, not the 0.60 m of wire.

questions.text: A 0.10 m length of wire in a 0.30 T field feels a force of 45 mN. Calculate the current.
A wire of resistance 4.0 Ω is connected to a 6.0 V supply. 0.25 m of it is at right angles to a field of 0.080 T. Calculate the force on that length.
One side of a coil of 50 turns lies in a field of 0.12 T; the side is 8.0 cm long and carries 2.0 A. Calculate the force on that side of the coil (all 50 wires).
walkthrough: (one wire: $0.0192$ N; fifty of them: $0.96$ N)

questions.text: The magnetic flux density at a distance d from a small magnet is given by B = K ÷ d², where K is a constant. At d = 0.10 m, B = 640 μT. Calculate B at d = 0.20 m, in μT.
questions.hint: Find K first, then use it again — or notice doubling d divides B by 4.
walkthrough: Answer: $= 160$ μT — inverse square: twice the distance, a quarter of the field

questions.text: A student finds the constant K in the 2025-style question and stops. Out of 3 marks she scores…
questions.explain: The report: finding K 'earning 1 of 3, but made no further progress'.

checklist: Rearrange $F = BIl$ for any quantity and convert units first
Use only the length of wire inside the field
Use an unfamiliar given equation with the same care as a familiar one
sections.blurb: The harder $F = BIl$ questions hide one of three things: the length is only the part of the wire inside the field; the current comes from another equation first ($V = IR$); or the equation is an unfamiliar one you are given and simply have to use. In 2024 the answer was 0.58 T; in 2025 an inverse-square equation gave 160 μT.

sections.title: The d.c. motor: why the coil turns, and why it keeps turning

parts.title: The chain, then the commutator
parts.html:
The standard explanation of the motor effect in a motor, in the steps the marks are on (the Simple Motor page animates it):

  1. There is a current in the coil.
  2. This creates a magnetic field around the coil.
  3. This interacts with the permanent magnetic field.
  4. This causes a resultant force on the coil.
  5. The direction of the force is opposite on either side of the coil.
  6. So the coil rotates.

Why the forces are opposite: the current goes one way along one side of the coil and the opposite way along the other, and Fleming's left-hand rule gives opposite forces for opposite currents in the same field. The two forces make a turning effect about the axle.

The split-ring commutator: two half-rings on the axle, each joined to one end of the coil, turning with it; two fixed brushes press on them and connect to the supply. Every half turn the halves swap brushes, so the current in the coil reverses. Without it, once the coil passed the vertical the force on each side would be the same way as before but that side is now on the other side of the axle, so it would be turned back — the coil would rock to the vertical and stop. With it, the side that is now on the left always carries the current the left side needs, so the force on it is always the same way and the coil keeps turning in the same direction. The June 2025 report (Q6(c)): credit was given for "reversing the current every half turn" and for explaining that this "lets the motor spin continuously" (keeps rotating in the same direction); many gave the first without the second, some said it stops the wires tangling, and "a surprisingly large number" described a dynamo — one scored 1 of 3 because "the motor does not produce a current".

Faster (larger force): more current, a stronger magnet, more turns on the coil, an iron core in the coil. Reverse: reverse the current (swap the supply connections) or reverse the field (swap the magnets). The force on each side is the same size at every angle (the long sides are always at right angles to the field), but its turning effect is largest when the coil is flat and falls to zero as the coil reaches the vertical — real motors use several coils at different angles so there is never a dead spot.

parts.title: The 6-mark motor
parts.question: Explain how a simple d.c. motor produces continuous rotation. (6 marks)
steps: There is a current in the coil. This creates a magnetic field around the coil.
This interacts with the permanent magnetic field. This causes a resultant force on the coil.
The direction of the force is opposite on either side of the coil (the current goes opposite ways along the two sides — Fleming's left-hand rule). So the coil rotates.
The split-ring commutator turns with the coil; its two halves are connected to the ends of the coil and press against fixed brushes.
Every half turn the halves swap brushes, so the current in the coil reverses…
…so the force on whichever side is on the left is always in the same direction, and the coil keeps rotating in the same direction instead of rocking back.

questions.text: Explain why the coil of a d.c. motor starts to turn when the current is switched on. (4)
questions.model:
• There is a current in the coil. This creates a magnetic field around the coil.
  • This interacts with the permanent magnetic field. This causes a resultant force on the coil.
  • The direction of the force is opposite on either side of the coil (the current goes opposite ways along the two sides).
  • So the coil rotates (the two forces give a turning effect about the axle).

questions.text: Explain the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor. (3)
questions.model:
• It reverses the current in the coil every half turn (the halves of the ring swap brushes as the coil turns).
  • So the force on each side of the coil is always in the direction needed on that side of the axle…
  • …and the coil keeps rotating in the same direction (continuously) instead of turning back and stopping.

questions.text: Which statement about a d.c. motor is WRONG?
options: The forces on the two sides of the coil are in opposite directions
The commutator reverses the current every half turn
Reversing the supply reverses the rotation
questions.explain: 2025 report: 'the motor does not produce a current' — that is a generator (Topic 13).

questions.text: State two changes that would make the coil of a d.c. motor turn faster. (2)
questions.model:
• Increase the current (higher pd) — or use stronger magnets.
  • More turns on the coil (or an iron core) — each gives a larger force and so a larger turning effect.

questions.text: What would happen to a motor's coil if the split ring were replaced by a complete ring (the same connection all the time)?
options: It would turn to the vertical, then be pushed back — rocking about the vertical and stopping
It would turn the other way
questions.explain: Without reversal the force turns the coil back once it passes vertical.

questions.text: A student describes a d.c. motor by writing: "As the coil turns in the field, a current is induced in it, which makes it spin." Explain the error. (2)
questions.model:
• That describes a generator/dynamo (electromagnetic induction): a motor does not produce a current.
  • In a motor the current comes from the supply; the force on the current-carrying coil in the field (the motor effect) makes it turn.

checklist: Write the six-step chain for the motor effect in a motor
Explain what the split-ring commutator does and why the motor needs it
State what makes the motor turn faster, and what reverses it
sections.blurb: A motor is the motor effect applied to a coil: the current goes one way along one side and the other way along the opposite side, so the forces are opposite and the coil turns. The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn so that it keeps turning the same way. In 2025 the commutator was 'poorly explained' and many students described a generator instead.

sections.title: Investigating an electromagnet: the seven steps, and describing the trend

parts.title: The recipe applied

Describing the trend (June 2025 Q7(b)(iii)): "as the number of turns increases the number of nails held increases" scores; better answers added that the increase is not linear (not proportional — the graph is not a straight line through the origin). The examiners: candidates "should be discouraged from using the term 'inversely proportional'" as a synonym for "one goes down as the other goes up" — it only means that one variable is proportional to the reciprocal of the other. Say what happens to the dependent variable as the independent variable increases, and whether the change is steady, speeding up or levelling off.

Afterwards the nails may have become weak permanent magnets (steel), which would change later counts — hence the 2025 test for permanent magnetism (T2).

parts.title: The 6-mark plan
parts.question: Plan an investigation to find how the strength of an electromagnet depends on the number of turns of wire on its core. (6 marks)
steps: Variables: change the number of turns (independent); measure the strength as the number of nails the electromagnet can hold (dependent); keep the current, the core and the nails the same (control).

Relationship expected: more turns, a stronger electromagnet, so more nails held (no equation needed). Circuit: the coil in series with a cell, a switch, an ammeter and a variable resistor, set so the current is the same for every number of turns.
Change: wind 10 turns on the iron core; then 20, 30, 40, 50 — five values at least.
Measure: switch on, lower the core into a tray of nails, lift it out and count the nails held; switch off between readings.
Use: plot number of nails against number of turns and describe the trend.
Accuracy and repeats: use the same tray of nails and lift from the same depth each time; repeat each number of turns three times and take a mean.
