sections.blurb: The 2025 paper used nails picked up by an electromagnet as the measure of its strength, against the number of turns. The seven-step recipe from Topic 1 (T6 there) plans it; the data question wants a trend described in plain words — not 'inversely proportional', which the examiners said to avoid unless it is true.

facts.q: Rule for poles?
facts.a: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

facts.q: Why is attraction not a test for a magnet?
facts.a: A magnet attracts any magnetic material (it induces the opposite pole), whichever way round. Only repulsion proves an object is a magnet.

facts.q: The 2-mark 'is it a magnet' test?
facts.a: Bring the same pole of a known magnet to each end in turn (test both orientations) AND state the result: a magnet is repelled at one end; a magnetic material is attracted at both.

facts.q: The four magnetic materials?
facts.a: Iron, steel, cobalt, nickel.

facts.q: Permanent magnet?
facts.a: Produces its own magnetic field all the time (steel).

facts.q: Induced (temporary) magnet?
facts.a: A magnetic material that is a magnet only while in a field; loses it when the field is removed (soft iron).

facts.q: Which pole is induced nearest a magnet's N pole?
facts.a: A S pole — so induced magnetism always attracts.

facts.q: Why iron, not steel, for an electromagnet core?
facts.a: Iron loses its magnetism when the current is off, so the electromagnet can be switched off; steel would stay magnetised.

facts.q: Use of a permanent magnet? Of a temporary one?
facts.a: Permanent: compass needle, motor, loudspeaker, fridge magnet. Temporary: electromagnet core, relay, electric bell, transformer core.

facts.q: What is a magnetic field?
facts.a: The region around a magnet (or current) where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force.

facts.q: Which way do field lines point?
facts.a: Out of N, into S (outside the magnet).

facts.q: How does a diagram show field strength?
facts.a: Closer lines = stronger field; closest at the poles.

facts.q: Field between N and S poles facing each other?
facts.a: Uniform: straight, parallel, equally spaced lines from N to S.

facts.q: Three ways to lose the field-diagram marks?
facts.a: Lines that cross or touch; no arrows; arrows into N.

facts.q: How to plot a field line with a compass?
facts.a: Mark dots at each end of the needle; move the compass so its tail is on the head's dot; repeat; join the dots; arrow the way the N end pointed.

facts.q: What does a compass pointing north show?
facts.a: The Earth has a magnetic field, so its core must be magnetic (like a bar magnet inside the Earth).

facts.q: Which magnetic pole is near geographic north?
facts.a: A magnetic S pole — the compass's N pole is attracted to it.

facts.q: Shape of the field around a straight wire?
facts.a: Concentric circles centred on the wire, further apart with distance.

facts.q: Right-hand grip rule?
facts.a: Thumb along the (conventional) current; fingers curl the way the field goes.

facts.q: Current out of the page: field direction?
facts.a: Anticlockwise (into the page: clockwise).

facts.q: What does the strength of a wire's field depend on?
facts.a: The size of the current (more = stronger) and the distance from the wire (further = weaker).

facts.q: How to show a current has a magnetic effect?
facts.a: Wire through a card with plotting compasses: they line up in circles when the current is on and reverse when it is reversed.

facts.q: Field inside a solenoid?
facts.a: Strong and almost uniform: the fields of the turns add together along the centre.

facts.q: Field outside a solenoid?
facts.a: Weaker: the fields of the turns largely cancel; the shape is a bar magnet's.

facts.q: Three ways to make an electromagnet stronger?
facts.a: More current, more turns, an iron core.

facts.q: What does reversing the current in a solenoid do?
facts.a: Swaps its N and S poles.

facts.q: The motor effect?
facts.a: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, due to the interaction between the two magnetic fields.

facts.q: The five-step chain for a wire?
facts.a: Current in the wire → magnetic field around the wire → interacts with the permanent field → resultant force, so the wire accelerates → direction from Fleming's left-hand rule.

facts.q: What force acts on the magnet?
facts.a: An equal and opposite force (Newton's third law).

facts.q: When is the motor-effect force zero? Largest?
facts.a: Zero when the wire is parallel to the field; largest at right angles.

facts.q: The 'interaction' mark (2023 Q5(b))?
facts.a: 'Repulsion' alone scored 1; the second mark was 'the interaction between the two magnetic fields'.

facts.q: Fleming's left-hand rule: the three digits?
facts.a: First finger: Field (N → S). Second finger: Current (+ → −). Thumb: Motion (force).

facts.q: Dot and cross?
facts.a: Dot: current out of the page (towards you). Cross: into the page.

facts.q: Two ways to reverse the force on a wire?
facts.a: Reverse the current, or reverse the field (turn the magnet round). Both together: no change.

facts.q: Which current direction does the second finger use?
facts.a: Conventional current, + to − (not electron flow).

facts.q: Equation for the force on a wire at right angles to a field?
facts.a: $F = B I l$: force (N) = flux density (T) × current (A) × length in the field (m).

facts.q: Unit of magnetic flux density?
facts.a: Tesla, T (= N/A m).

facts.q: Three F = BIl traps?
facts.a: cm not converted to m; using the whole wire instead of the length in the field; forgetting F = 0 for a wire parallel to the field.

facts.q: Chain for a magnet moving away from another?
facts.a: The two fields interact → like poles repel, so a force on X away from Y → X accelerates away.

facts.q: Chain for a floating magnet?
facts.a: Fields interact → repulsive (upward) force on the upper magnet → equal to its weight, so the forces are balanced and it stays still.

facts.q: Why is iron always attracted, never repelled?
facts.a: The magnet induces the opposite pole in the near end of the iron, whichever pole faces it.

facts.q: What does 'picks up a paper clip' prove?
facts.a: Only that it is magnetised now — possibly induced. Repulsion by a known magnet is the proof of a permanent magnet.

facts.q: Result that shows a nail is NOT a permanent magnet?
facts.a: No repulsion in either orientation (attraction the same at both ends, or none).

facts.q: Field between two like poles facing?
facts.a: Lines curve away from each other; a neutral point midway where the field is zero.

facts.q: What earns the two marks on a field diagram?
facts.a: Shape: separate, non-crossing lines, pole to pole, closer at the poles. Direction: arrows out of N into S.

facts.q: Direction of the Earth's field at the equator?
facts.a: Parallel to the surface, pointing (geographic) north.

facts.q: Where do the Earth's field lines go into the Earth?
facts.a: Near the geographic north pole (the magnetic S pole); out near geographic south.

facts.q: The 2024 three marks of evidence?
facts.a: Earth has a magnetic field; the compass points along the field; the core is magnetic / as if a magnet were inside the Earth (or a point read from the diagram).

facts.q: Field left → right, current out of the page: force?
facts.a: Up the page.

facts.q: Field left → right, current into the page: force?
facts.a: Down the page.

facts.q: Wire along the field lines: force?
facts.a: Zero.

facts.q: How much of a long wire counts in F = BIl?
facts.a: Only the length inside the field (e.g. the width of the poles).

facts.q: Force on a coil side with N turns?
facts.a: $N$ × the force on one wire: $F = B I l N$.

facts.q: The 2025 unfamiliar equation?
facts.a: B against distance, inverse square (B ∝ 1/d²); use it like any other — finding the constant alone was 1 of 3.

facts.q: The six-step chain for a motor?
facts.a: Current in the coil → field around the coil → interacts with the permanent field → resultant force on the coil → force opposite on either side → so the coil rotates.

facts.q: What does the split-ring commutator do?
facts.a: Reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction.

facts.q: What happens with no commutator?
facts.a: The coil turns to the vertical, is pushed back, and rocks to a stop.

facts.q: Three ways to make a motor turn faster?
facts.a: More current, stronger magnets, more turns (or an iron core).

facts.q: The 2025 motor trap?
facts.a: Describing a dynamo: 'the motor does not produce a current' — the current comes from the supply.

facts.q: Dependent variable in the electromagnet investigation?
facts.a: Its strength, measured as the number of nails (or clips) held, or the mass lifted.

facts.q: Why not say 'inversely proportional' for a falling trend?
facts.a: It only means proportional to the reciprocal; say 'as X increases, Y decreases' and whether it is linear.

facts.q: Why switch the electromagnet off between readings?
facts.a: So the coil does not heat up (changing the current) and the nails do not become permanent magnets.

facts.q: State what is meant by: magnetic material.
facts.a: A material that is attracted by a magnet and can be magnetised: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel.

facts.q: State what is meant by: permanent magnet.
facts.a: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time (steel, or alloys of cobalt and nickel).

facts.q: State what is meant by: induced (temporary) magnet.
facts.a: A magnetic material that becomes a magnet only while it is in a magnetic field, and loses its magnetism when the field is removed (soft iron).

facts.q: State what is meant by: magnetic field.
facts.a: The region around a magnet (or a current) in which a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force.

facts.q: State what is meant by: field line.
facts.a: A line showing the direction of the field (the direction of the force on a N pole: N to S); closer lines mean a stronger field; lines never cross.

facts.q: State what is meant by: uniform field.
facts.a: A field with the same strength and direction everywhere: parallel, equally spaced lines (between unlike poles; inside a solenoid).

facts.q: State what is meant by: solenoid.
facts.a: A long coil of wire; with a current it has a field like a bar magnet's, strong and uniform inside.

facts.q: State what is meant by: electromagnet.
facts.a: A solenoid with a soft iron core: a magnet that can be switched on and off with the current.

facts.q: State what is meant by: right-hand grip rule.
facts.a: Grip the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current: the fingers curl the way the field goes.

facts.q: State what is meant by: motor effect.
facts.a: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, due to the interaction between the two magnetic fields.

facts.q: State what is meant by: Fleming's left-hand rule.
facts.a: First finger Field (N → S), second finger Current (+ → −), thumb Motion (force), all at right angles.

facts.q: State what is meant by: magnetic flux density, B.
facts.a: The strength of a magnetic field: the force per unit current per unit length on a wire at right angles to it; unit tesla, T (= N/A m).

facts.q: State what is meant by: split-ring commutator.
facts.a: The two half-rings on a d.c. motor's axle that reverse the current in the coil every half turn, so the coil keeps turning the same way.

types.name: Force on a current-carrying conductor
types.method: The force on a wire at right angles to a magnetic field is magnetic flux density multiplied by current multiplied by the length of wire in the field. B is in tesla, I in amps and l in metres, so change cm to m (divide by 100) first. The equation is on the equation sheet; to find B, I or l, divide F by the other two.
commonErrors: Leaving the length in cm, so the force is 100 times too big
Mixing up B (flux density, in T) and F (force, in N)
Forgetting that the force is zero if the wire runs along the field rather than across it

worked.question: A straight wire 0.5 m long carries a current of 3 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.4 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
steps: Known: B = 0.4 T, I = 3 A, l = 0.5 m. Unknown: F.
F = B × I × l
